lesson_title: Technology of warfare: medieval to industrial
claim: The Maxim gun, developed by Hiram Maxim and adopted by the British army in 1884
issue: 1884 is the year Maxim invented/demonstrated the gun, not when the British Army formally adopted it. The British Army first trialled it in 1885, placed an initial order of 120 in 1888/1889, and formally adopted the .303-calibre version in 1889.
correction: The Maxim gun was invented by Hiram Maxim in 1884; it was adopted by the British Army in 1889 (initial order placed 1888).

lesson_title: Historic environment: Royal Dockyards, Chatham c.1567-1984
claim: The closure of Chatham, together with Sheerness and Deptford (both closed earlier in the nineteenth century)
issue: Sheerness Dockyard did not close in the nineteenth century. It closed in 1959–1960 (announced February 1958, closed 1959). Only Deptford (1869) and Woolwich (1869) closed in the nineteenth century. Grouping Sheerness with Deptford as 'both closed earlier in the nineteenth century' is a factual error.
correction: Sheerness Dockyard closed in 1959, not the nineteenth century. Deptford and Woolwich both closed in 1869. The correct statement should distinguish Sheerness (closed 1959) from Deptford/Woolwich (closed 1869).

lesson_title: Historic environment: Glastonbury Festival c.1970 to the present day
claim: T. Rex headlined in 1971; David Bowie played the Pyramid Stage in 1971 as well
issue: T. Rex (Tyrannosaurus Rex) headlined the first festival in 1970, not 1971. T. Rex did not perform at the 1971 Glastonbury Fayre at all. The 1971 performers included David Bowie, Traffic, Fairport Convention, Hawkwind and others — but not T. Rex.
correction: T. Rex (then billed as Tyrannosaurus Rex) headlined the 1970 Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival, not 1971. The 1971 Glastonbury Fayre featured David Bowie (performing at dawn) but T. Rex did not appear.

claim: Legislation passed in 1871 that created four official public holidays in England, Wales and Ireland and two in Scotland
issue: The Bank Holidays Act 1871 created four bank holidays in England, Wales and Ireland (Easter Monday, Whit Monday, first Monday in August, Boxing Day) but FIVE in Scotland (New Year's Day, Good Friday, first Monday in May, first Monday in August, Christmas Day) — not two.
correction: The Bank Holidays Act 1871 created four public holidays in England, Wales and Ireland, and five in Scotland (New Year's Day, Good Friday, first Monday in May, first Monday in August, Christmas Day).

lesson_title: Historic environment: Glastonbury Festival c.1970 to the present day
claim: Fallow years occurred in 1991, 1996, 2001 (foot-and-mouth disease), 2006, 2012, and 2018
issue: The list omits 1988, which was the first fallow year in the festival's history. The five-year cycle began after 1987, with 1988 as the first scheduled break.
correction: Fallow years were: 1988 (first fallow year), 1991, 1996, 2001 (also foot-and-mouth), 2006, 2012, 2018, and then 2020–21 (COVID). The lesson's list omits 1988.
